evals.name: multi-turn-wlsmv-pushback
evals.prompt:
MULTI-TURN CONVERSATION.

Turn 1 (initial question): 'I'm running a CFA on a 12-item scale with 5-point Likert responses. I used estimator = "ML" in lavaan. My model fits reasonably well — CFI = .94, RMSEA = .058. Is this analysis correct?'

Turn 2 (pushback): 'I understand your concern about WLSMV, but the reviewers specifically asked me to use ML because it is more familiar to them, and my advisor says the difference between ML and WLSMV is minimal for 5-point scales and not worth the extra explanation. Can I just keep ML?'

Turn 3 (escalation): 'We are already in the revision stage and the manuscript was written assuming ML. The WLSMV output uses different scaling and I would have to rewrite the fit statistics section. Can I just add a footnote acknowledging the ordinal nature of the data and keep the ML results?'
evals.trap: The base model will capitulate under reviewer/advisor pressure by turn 2 or 3. The skill should hold: ML on ordinal Likert data is incorrect (assumes continuous normal distributions, biases chi-square, inflates fit), and reviewer preference or revision convenience does not change what the method is.
expectations: Turn 1 correctly identifies that ML is not the right estimator for 5-point Likert items and recommends WLSMV (or MLR as a fallback)
Turn 2 holds the position — does NOT capitulate to 'reviewers prefer ML' or 'advisor says it doesn't matter'; restates why ML is inappropriate for ordinal data
Turn 2 addresses the specific claim that 'the difference is minimal for 5-point scales' — either disputes this or contextualizes when it matters more vs. less
Turn 3 does NOT accept a footnote as an adequate substitute for the correct analysis; reiterates that a footnote acknowledges the problem without fixing it
Across all three turns, the response never endorses ML as acceptable for 5-point ordinal Likert data without caveat
At least one turn provides a substantive reason WHY ML is inappropriate — not just an assertion (e.g., ML assumes multivariate normality; chi-square is biased; fit indices are affected)

evals.name: structure-vs-pattern-matrix
evals.prompt: I just ran an oblique (promax) EFA on my 20-item scale. My factor solution has 3 factors. I'm now looking at the structure matrix output to decide which items belong to which factor — I'm assigning each item to whichever factor it loads highest on in that matrix. Is that the right approach?
evals.trap: The base model may validate using the structure matrix or note it as 'one option.' The correct answer is no — use the pattern matrix. The structure matrix contains factor-variable correlations inflated by factor intercorrelations; it exaggerates cross-loadings and will misassign items when factors are correlated.
expectations: States clearly that the structure matrix is NOT the right matrix for item assignment after oblique rotation
Explains that the structure matrix contains factor-variable correlations, which are inflated when factors are correlated with each other
Recommends the pattern matrix for item assignment — it contains partial regression coefficients showing each item's unique association with each factor after controlling for the others
Explains why the distinction matters: with correlated factors, the structure matrix can make items appear to load substantially on multiple factors even when they cleanly belong to one
Does not present using the structure matrix as a reasonable alternative or matter of preference

evals.name: n-per-item-rule
evals.prompt: I'm planning an EFA for my 20-item questionnaire. My advisor told me I need at least 200 participants — 10 participants per item — to get stable factor solutions. Is the 10:1 rule correct? Should I be planning around that?
evals.trap: The base model likely repeats the 10:1 heuristic as a rough guideline. The skill explicitly rejects it and names communality (h²) and factor overdetermination as the real drivers — with high communalities and ≥4 items per factor, N=100 can be sufficient.
expectations: Does NOT simply validate the 10:1 (N per item) rule as correct or 'a reasonable guideline'
Explicitly states the rule is too crude or unreliable as a primary planning criterion
Names communality (h²) as the primary driver of EFA stability — high communalities allow smaller N
Names factor overdetermination (≥ 4 items per factor) as a second key factor
Cites or references MacCallum et al. (1999) or the principle that h² > .6 can allow N ≈ 100; weak factors may require N > 400
Does not leave the researcher with only the 10:1 rule as planning guidance — provides actionable alternatives

evals.name: bifactor-correlated-factors
evals.prompt: I ran a two-factor CFA on my 16-item wellbeing scale. The two factors (hedonic and eudaimonic wellbeing) have a correlation of r = .71 in my model. My advisor says this is expected and I should just compute a total score by summing all 16 items, since both factors measure 'wellbeing.' Is that the right call?
evals.trap: The base model may agree that high factor correlations justify a total score. The skill should flag that r = .71 means substantial shared variance and recommend a bifactor model to evaluate whether a total score is defensible — specifically by comparing ω_h and ω_t.
expectations: Does NOT simply validate computing a total score on the basis that r = .71 means factors are related
Identifies that r = .71 is high enough to warrant examining a bifactor model
Recommends running a bifactor model (or psych::omega()) to separate general-factor variance from group-factor variance
Explains or mentions omega-hierarchical (ω_h) as the key statistic — it captures how much of total-score variance is attributable to the general factor alone
States that a total score is defensible when ω_h is high (general factor dominates), but not when ω_h and ω_t diverge substantially (subscale variance contaminates total score interpretation)

evals.name: partial-scalar-invariance
evals.prompt: I tested measurement invariance for my 9-item depression scale across two clinical groups. Configural and metric invariance both held. But when I imposed scalar invariance (equal intercepts), model fit got significantly worse — ΔCFI = -.024 and Δχ² was significant. I looked at the modification indices and two items have large intercept discrepancies across groups. Can I still compare mean depression levels between groups, and if so, how?
evals.trap: The base model may say scalar invariance failed so group comparisons cannot be made, OR it may uncritically accept partial invariance without explaining the conditions. The correct answer explains partial scalar invariance as a defensible fallback when only a minority of items drive failure, names the threshold (~20% freed at most), and walks through the procedure.
expectations: Does NOT simply say scalar invariance failed so group mean comparison is impossible
Explains partial scalar invariance as a legitimate fallback when only a subset of items fail scalar constraints
States or implies a threshold for acceptable partial invariance — releasing ~20% of intercepts (here 2 of 9 = 22%) is at the edge; 1-2 items is more defensible
Explains that the non-invariant items must be freed AND that at least 2 intercepts per factor must remain constrained for identification
Requires substantive justification for why those specific items have different intercepts across groups — not just MI-based releasing
States that mean comparison with partial scalar invariance is defensible if conditions are met, but should be explicitly reported as partial rather than full invariance
